a shift toward a smaller hemithorax indicates volume loss (hypoplasia/atelectasis), whereas a shift away suggests a space-occupying lesion (mass/effusion).", "Inspect the lung parenchyma for signs of hypoplasia, such as lobar aplasia, reduced vascular markings, or anomalous venous drainage (e.g., scimitar vein), rather than acute consolidation or large fluid collections.", "Differentiate between primary volume loss causing the shift versus secondary compensatory hyperinflation of the contralateral lung pushing the mediastinum; in hypoplasia, the ipsilateral deficit is the primary driver."]}, {"category": "reasoning", "trigger": "When evaluating a frontal chest X-ray showing left superior mediastinal widening and mild cardiomegaly in a patient with unexplained hypoxaemia or dyspnoea.", "steps": ["Identify the specific location of mediastinal widening: confirm it is localized to the left superior mediastinum (often appearing as a vertical density parallel to the aortic knob) rather than a diffuse mass or right-sided deviation.", "Assess the lung fields for signs of pulmonary congestion or edema; note if they are clear despite the presence of cardiac silhouette enlargement.", "Correlate the anatomical finding (widened left superior mediastinum) with the physiological symptom (hypoxaemia) by considering a Persistent Left Superior Vena Cava (PLSVC) draining into the left atrium.", "Distinguish this from left heart failure (which would typically show pulmonary venous congestion) or compressive masses (which would not inherently cause shunting/hypoxaemia without airway compromise)."]}]
